title: Star forming region, NGC 206
caption: The star-forming region NGC 206 in the Andromeda Galaxy, imaged by the WIYN 0.9-meter telescope
credit: T.A. Rector and A. Strom (University of Alaska Anchorage) and WIYN

recognition.text: Published in the NSF NOIRLab image archive. No published rating.

story: A bluish patch of stars sits between the center and upper-left corner of this view of the Andromeda Galaxy, M31. This is NGC 206, a massive star-forming region embedded in Andromeda, of the kind called an OB association. Scattered red nebulae mark other places in the galaxy where stars are forming right now.
NGC 206 is estimated to contain about 200,000 times the mass of our Sun. Its distinctive blue color comes from very young, hot and massive stars.

Those stars also reveal its age. Massive stars burn through their fuel quickly and do not last long, so their presence shows that the cluster has existed for less than 10 million years, extremely young for stars. An OB association is a loose grouping of these short-lived O and B type stars, born around the same time from the same region of gas.

understand.summary: The Mosaic camera on the WIYN 0.9-meter telescope observed this part of Andromeda in visible light through B, V and hydrogen-alpha filters, shown as blue, green and red respectively.
filters: 436 nm · Optical B (WIYN 0.9-meter Telescope Mosaic I)
537 nm · Optical V (WIYN 0.9-meter Telescope Mosaic I)
656 nm · Optical Ha (WIYN 0.9-meter Telescope Mosaic I)
understand.eye: The hydrogen-alpha filter isolates the red glow of star-forming gas, bringing out nebulae that the eye could not pick out in the galaxy's overall light.

explore: The image was obtained with the wide-field Mosaic camera on the WIYN 0.9-meter telescope at Kitt Peak National Observatory. It is oriented with north at the bottom and east to the right.
alt: Part of a spiral galaxy with a bright bluish cluster of stars near the center to upper left and scattered small red nebulae.
